parts:
I have a (mixture) model with a few latent Gaussian processes, and as you might expect, instantiation is a pain. I generated a toy dataset, and if I the initial parameters to the ground truth of what they should be, sampling still works (though it's pretty darn slow) but I'm not confident (even after running for 5K warmup iterations) I've converged to the stationary distribution. messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] term
parts:
MCMC is more robust than ADVI or MAP and also computes
the reference result. ADVI is an approximation, but the
code's not very robust in Stan to fit. MAP computes something
different, and a MAP solution might not exist in many cases
(like hierarchical models) where the posterior mode is well
defined.

What do you mean by "instantiation" when you say it's a pain?
Initialization? Did you try default inits?

All of HMC, ADVI, and L-BFGS use gradient information, but
the algorithms are totally different. Also, ADVI isn't very
robust. And L-BFGS won't find a mode where one doesn't
exist.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] term
parts:
What happens under random inits? Do you get -infinity log
density? Or does it fail with an exception somewhere? The
latter usually indicates a bug in the coding, usually missing
constraints on parameters. All parameter values satisfying
the declared constraints should have support (finite log density)
in the model.

The other common problem in GPs is lack of jitter---trying to make
the model too deterministic.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] term
parts:
I don't see any error message there. Are you using the latest
PyStan? This may just mean that some of the arithmetic underflows
to zero before having log assigned.

You can print out target() as you go:

...

and so on to try to figure out where the negative infinity is getting
introduced. It may be that some of the arithmetic can be made
more robust by working directly on the log scale.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] term
parts: Turns out you were correct in saying that working directly on the log-scale can make the arithmetic more robust. Specifically, the Cholesky parametrized normal likelihood was the issue, and using the following representation directly (dropping the 2pi constant) lets the model run (even with opt, haven't tried out vb yet though will report back when I do). I wonder if this was a problem with using the Sigma = LL' factorization when L didn't have positive diagonal entries, and therefore wasn't the _Cholesky_ factorization, even though the math could be the same. If Stan assumes that the diagonal elements are positive, the log determinant could be computed more efficiently (see below: the square in L_ii^2 could be brought out of the sum as a scaling factor). In that case, taking the log of L_ii could be undefined (in the real plane) and return infinity or something. Does Stan do this under the hood?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] term
parts:
Yes, the determinant calculation for the Cholesky-parameterized
multi-normal is done efficiently. Ben keeps a close watch on
our linear algebra for critical functions like this.

The relevant code for the determinant is in

stan/math/prim/mat/prob/multi_normal_cholesky_lpdf.hpp

and looks just like you'd expect for Cholesky factor L and
log density accumulator lp (recall the determinant is in
the denominator of the density).

lp -= L.diagonal().array().log().sum() * size_vec;

size_vec is the number of variates, so that we only compute
this determinant once if it's called with an array of
variates. That is, if we call y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L) and y
is an array of vectors. Then rather than computing it and adding
it for each vector element of y, we just multiply.

Also, we use template traits programming to wrap this in a static
conditional that only includes the decrement if the matrix L
isn't data. If it's data, the result is a constant term and is
dropped.

We also use specialized arithmetic to compute the quadratic form
using matrix division that's specialized for a triangular matrix,
where this gets called in a loop for each y in the sequence
of variates (may just be one if the argument isn't an array of
vectors):

sum_lp_vec += dot_self(mdivide_left_tri_low(L, y_minus_mu));

and then the whole result gets multiplied at once and subtracted
from the accumulator:

lp -= 0.5 * sum_lp_vec;

Eigen's great!

- Bob
